questions: Does slalom progress exceed the iteration 1 level of 0.18, and at what bend does the robot now leave the tape?
Does the narrower wheel track raise steering_oscillation or cause instability at speed on the oval, which previously finished?
Does the controller saturate the wheel commands (turn at the limit of ±350 PWM per unit) on the tightest bends with the 0.10 m track?
Compared with iteration 1, does the s-bend finish rate increase from 8 of 20?

intent: Return to the best-measured sensor array (iteration 1) and test a narrower wheel track (0.10 m) to add turn authority on the slalom and s-bend corners where the robot currently leaves the tape. Every other geometry value is held fixed so the result isolates wheel track.
learning: Iteration 3 (±0.04 m, 20 mm spacing) reduced performance on every track, with oval falling from 1.0 finish rate to 0.0. Wider sensor spacing is therefore harmful at this resolution, and the 12 mm spacing of iteration 1 should be kept. Hypothesis H1: a narrower wheel track increases yaw rate per unit of wheel differential, which reduces max_error on tight bends. Check H1 through max_error and line_loss_events on slalom and s-bend. Hypothesis H2: the iteration 1 array remains the best sensor layout, so further changes should be made to drive geometry rather than to sensor spacing.
rationale: The race evidence in entityR2A points at sensor reach and array resolution. Iteration 1 (five 16 mm sensors at 12 mm spacing, x = ±0.024 m, y = 0.05 m, mass 0.5 kg, wheel radius 0.03 m) finished the oval in 20 of 20 trials and 8 of 20 s-bend trials, with the best overall score of 525.5. Iteration 3 widened the array to ±0.04 m at 20 mm spacing, and the result fell to 127.5. The oval failed in 20 of 20 trials at progress 0.43, so the wider spacing degraded the signal on the track where iteration 1 was already working. The 20 mm gaps and coarser weight resolution appear to hurt more than the extra reach helps. I therefore restore the iteration 1 sensor array, which is the best measured geometry, and change one variable: wheel_track 0.12 to 0.10 m. For a given wheel-speed difference, a narrower track gives a higher turn rate (turn rate = wheel speed difference / wheel_track), which should help the tight slalom and s-bend corners where iteration 1 left the tape. Mass, wheel radius, body and sensor layout stay as in iteration 1, so any change in result can be attributed to wheel track. Body width has no effect below 0.18 m because the off-track floor of 0.06 m governs, so it stays at 0.12 m. Expected result: slalom and s-bend progress rise above their iteration 1 values (0.18 and 0.83), and line_loss_events and max_error fall, while the oval finish rate holds at 1.0. The risk is that a narrower track reduces stability at speed, so steering_oscillation may rise.
